title: U.S. goods and services trade deficit, June 2026
question: What will the first-print U.S. goods and services trade deficit be for June 2026, seasonally adjusted and not price adjusted, in Exhibit 1 of the U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services release?
resolutionSource: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services release
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first official June 2026 value for the goods and services deficit in Exhibit 1, seasonally adjusted and not price adjusted, reported in billions of dollars. Use the first print released on August 4, 2026; ignore later revisions. If the table reports balance as a negative number, convert the deficit to a positive usd_billions value using the absolute value, rounded to one decimal place.
drivers: May deficit widened sharply to $77.6 billion on lower exports and higher imports
January-April 2026 deficits clustered near $54-$57 billion before the May jump
Services surplus has been stable near $28-$29 billion, so goods volatility dominates the forecast
May import strength in consumer goods, autos, crude oil, semiconductors, and pharmaceuticals raises the June baseline
Some reversal of May's nonmonetary-gold export drag should narrow the deficit from May

reasoning.text: U.S. goods and services trade deficit, June 2026 first print

Framing and exact resolver: this forecast targets the BEA/Census U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services Exhibit 1 goods and services deficit for June 2026, seasonally adjusted and not price adjusted. Exhibit 1 reports balance as negative millions of dollars; this cell resolves to the positive deficit in usd_billions on the first print.

reasoning.call: Checked BEA release schedule for the June 2026 U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services release date.
reasoning.result: BEA schedule lists U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, June 2026 on August 4, 2026 at 8:30 AM; the schedule page was last modified 7/9/26.

reasoning.call: Checked BEA series landing page for latest release status and headline figures.
reasoning.result: The BEA page shows U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, May 2026: May deficit -$77.6B, April deficit -$54.6B, current release July 7, 2026, next release August 4, 2026.

reasoning.call: Read the July 7, 2026 full release PDF headline and components.
reasoning.result: The release states the goods and services deficit was $77.6B in May, up $23.0B from $54.6B in April; May exports were $317.7B, down $10.5B, and May imports were $395.3B, up $12.5B.

reasoning.call: Read Exhibit 1 seasonally adjusted history for the same variant and table.
reasoning.result: Exhibit 1 balance totals in millions were: 2026 Jan -54,185; Feb -54,980; Mar -56,585; Apr revised -54,570; May -77,585; 2025 Jun -58,697; Jul -75,062; Aug -59,642; Sep -59,392; Oct -37,376; Nov -63,868; Dec -76,078.

reasoning.text: Base rate/reference class: using the same Exhibit 1 seasonally adjusted not price adjusted deficit variant, the last 12 available monthly deficits from June 2025 through May 2026 average about $60.7B, while the first five months of 2026 average about $59.6B and the March-May 2026 moving average is $62.9B.

Level and momentum: May's $77.6B deficit is a high starting point, but January-April 2026 were tightly grouped at $54.2B, $55.0B, $56.6B, and $54.6B. I treat May as partly persistent because imports rose to $395.3B, but partly temporary because exports fell by $10.5B and nonmonetary gold alone decreased $6.2B in exports.

Policy/mechanism update: tariff and sourcing uncertainty can keep goods imports lumpy, especially semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, autos, and crude oil. The services surplus is much smoother, rising only from $28.3B in April to $28.9B in May, so the June uncertainty is mostly a goods-balance question.

Prior/update/interval: persistence prior is a blend of the latest deficit $77.6B, the 3-month average $62.9B, and the 12-month same-variant reference class mean $60.7B. Adjustment components: start near $67B from partial mean reversion, add about $2B for elevated imports and tariff/front-loading risk, subtract about $0B net for services stability, giving a $69.0B point. For the 80% interval, because this is a monthly flow/deficit amount, compute cross-sectional monthly level dispersion, not one-step forecast error volatility, from the fetched 12 monthly deficit values themselves: sigma = 10.4; half-width = 1.28*sigma = 1.28*10.4 = 13.3, so $69.0B +/- $13.4B gives about $55.6B to $82.4B.

Counter-considerations: upside risk is another import surge in semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, autos, or energy with weak exports, which would land above the interval. Downside risk is a reversal of May's gold/export weakness plus import payback after tariff-related front-loading, which would land below the interval. A value outside the interval would most likely require a second consecutive goods shock rather than services movement.

Review disposition: accepted the clarification that the interval uses cross-sectional monthly level dispersion over June 2025-May 2026 rather than one-step forecast error volatility, and kept the absolute-value resolver language because it removes sign ambiguity while preserving the ledger target.
